1: # Paint a picture
2: 
3: Compose and paint one original picture in the manner of Caspar David
4: Friedrich, at the easel, a simulator of oil paint on linen. The place,
5: subject and composition are yours to invent. Work from knowledge and the
6: notes in your studio; don't use reference images, image models or pictures
7: of his work.
8: 
9: ## Your studio
10: - The folder [local path redacted] this brief, your notes and the easel.
11: - The easel's tools are `paint`, `look`, `note`, `status` and `log`;
12:   notes/easel_guide.md explains them.
13: - There is no undo. To change a passage, paint over it, or lift wet
14:   paint with a rag or a brush.
15: - You mix your own paint on the palette, from the tubes, in the
16:   proportions you choose.
17: - Time passes on the painting's own clock: every mark takes the time a
18:   hand takes, and `wait(minutes)` lets it rest, as long as you like; paint
19:   dries as that time passes. Real time between chunks doesn't count.
20: 
21: ## The rules of the studio
22: - Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
23:   masks, amounts or proportions.
24: - Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by mirroring
25:   or rotating another mask's or stroke's coordinates. A shape that mirrors
26:   another is drawn as its own shape, not as `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or
27:   `m:at(W - x, y)`. Moving a shape and reusing your own helpers are fine.
28: 
29: ## What to read
30: notes/easel_guide.md; notes/techniques.md; notes/studio_notes.md;
31: notes/research/friedrich_materials.md (his materials and method, sourced) and
32: notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed.
33: 
34: After choosing a subject or technical question, use `reference` to search
35: the studio's reference library, or `reference_list` to browse its titles.
36: Read a result with `reference` by its id; follow next_page
37: until it is null to read the full text.
38: 
39: ## Working
40: Work one campaign at a time. After laying a campaign, inspect the whole picture in normal color and relevant detail before writing the code for the next campaign. Let what you see inform the next action; record what changes or why continuing unchanged serves the picture.
41: 
42: After the first large masses, consider whether the whole picture produces your intended effect: how its large shapes, values and spatial relationships support it, and whether anything weakens it. Before adding repeated small details, improve a weakening relationship or deliberately accept it with your reason. After a local repair, check its effect on the whole picture. If the repair recreates the problem, reconsider the composition or method before expanding it.
43: 
44: Before repeating an unfamiliar mixture or stroke, inspect a small trial, on the scratch canvas beside the painting (`scratch: true`) or on the painting, laid on the intended substrate after the intended treatment, alongside the existing marks in a detail crop. A held pile shows thick paint on steel; use the laid trial to judge its effect on the picture. For material trials and repairs, keep useful observations in your journal: substrate and wetness, recipe ratios, medium or thinner, brush load, coverage and the viewed result. Carry forward the conditions that mattered and label broader rules as hypotheses until a further trial isolates them.
45: 
46: - You make every artistic decision.
47: - Keep exploring what interests you. You’re free to reconsider a passage,
48:   change approach and discover where the painting can go.
49: - Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
50:   You can revise them.
51: - You may sign the painting.
52: - Take your time and enjoy painting. You can keep working for hours,
53:   exploring and revisiting passages until you are happy with the picture.
54: - An oil painting can develop over simulated years. Whether yours takes
55:   one simulated day or a thousand, that time is yours to use.
56: - When you feel ready to finish, use `look` to enjoy the whole painting
57:   and explore detail crops in normal color after your latest changes.
58:   Ask yourself: is your heart happy with this? Is there something you
59:   would enjoy taking further? Follow that interest for as long as you
60:   like. When you are happy with the painting, record your reflections
61:   in your journal and finish.
62: 
63: ## Your reply
64: When you stop working, reply with the painting's title if you give it one
65: and a few sentences about the picture.
66:

1: # The easel
2: 
3: The easel is a live oil painting. Its `paint` tool runs Lua chunks one at
4: a time; `look` shows the canvas. Under it is a physical paint simulator: simulated
5: bristles carry wet paint over a primed linen canvas, the paint levels and
6: dries on a clock, and layers combine by Kubelka–Munk optics.
7: 
8: Three things hold for every session:
9: 
10: - **Every chunk that runs stays on the canvas.** There is no undo. To
11:   change something, paint over it, lift wet paint off with a brush or
12:   a rag or scrape it off with a knife.
13: - **A chunk that stops with an error changes nothing.** The canvas, your
14:   variables, the paint on your brushes and the clock are as they were
15:   before it, and it isn't written to the log.
16: - **The log is the painting.** Every chunk that ran is appended to
17:   `paintings/lua/painting.lua`, and replaying it paints the same canvas.
18: 
19: ## Starting
20: 
21: The studio holds one painting, and the easel is open on it. Its tools:
22: 
23: | tool | what it does |
24: |---|---|
25: | `paint` | runs a chunk of Lua. The reply is what the chunk printed, the painting's current clock, then `ok` |
26: | `look` | shows you the canvas as it is now, or your palette (see [Looking](#looking)) |
27: | `note` | adds an entry to your journal (see [The journal](#the-journal)) |
28: | `status` | the canvas's setup |
29: | `log` | the painting so far: every chunk that ran, each after a line `--@ chunk` |
30: 
31: The first chunk is `canvas{}` (see [The canvas](#the-canvas)). `read` reads the files in this folder: your brief and
32: your notes.
33: 
34: Beside the painting is a scratch canvas to try things on (see [The scratch canvas](#the-scratch-canvas)): `paint`,
35: `look`, `status` and `log` work on it with `scratch: true`.
36: 
37: In the examples below, `<tube>` stands for a name from the tube box and
38: `<parts>` for a number of parts you choose. Other numbers in the examples
39: show how a call is written; the values are yours to choose.
40: 
41: ## The canvas
42: 
43: ```lua
44: canvas{size=<mm>, aspect=<width / height>, linen={<warp>, <weft>}, seed=<seed>,
45:        ground={{pile={{"<tube>", <parts>}, {"<tube>", <parts>}}, um=<µm>, apply="<how>", texture=<0..1>},
46:                ...}}
47: ```
48: 
49: - `size`: the canvas's width in mm (50 to 5000).
50: - `aspect`: width / height.
51: - `linen`: plain-weave linen, threads per cm, one number or `{warp, weft}`
52:   (4 to 60).
53: - `ground`: the preparation layers, bottom first. Each is a paste mixed
54:   from tubes in parts (as a pile is, below), a thickness in µm (5 to 400)
55:   and how it is put on: `"knife"` (levels the weave; `texture` 0..1 is the
56:   knife's waviness), `"roller"` (a fine even texture) or `"brush"` (laid in
57:   crossing strokes, its striations stay). The ground is dry when painting
58:   starts.
59: - `seed`: the randomness of the linen, the ground and everything after.
60: - `raw` (engine 3), instead of `ground`: leave the canvas raw, the bare
61:   cloth unprimed: `"cotton duck"` (creamy and absorbent) or `"linen"`
62:   (browner, it holds less). The cloth shows
63:   its color and its weave. A brush works on it as on a primed canvas: its
64:   paint lies on the cloth. `soaked(x, y)` says in words what is in the
65:   cloth there (`"raw"`), and whether paint lies on it.
66: - A ground layer's `absorbent=true` (or 0..1) makes it a chalk and glue
67:   ground: it draws oil out of the paint laid straight on it until its pores
68:   are full, so thin paint there goes lean, stiff, quick to set and matte,
69:   while thick paint barely notices. Paint that has dried over it seals it.
70:   An oil ground (the default) absorbs nothing and is semi-matte.
71: 
72: **Gloss.** Every dry surface is more or less glossy: oily paint (medium)
73: dries glossy, lean paint (blotted, or drawn out by an absorbent ground)
74: matte, a thin film shows the surface under it, a varnish makes all of it
75: glossy. A matte surface scatters the light its first surface reflects back
76: toward you, a faint veil of white over the colors that lifts the darks; a
77: glossy one sends it away. The looks show it.
78: 
79: It sets `W` (1000) and `H` (`1000 / aspect`). The canvas is always 1000
80: units wide, whatever its pixel width. The origin `(0, 0)` is the upper
81: left corner; x increases to the right and y downward. Angles are radians,
82: 0 left to right, π/2 downward.
83: 
84: ## Tubes and piles
85: 
86: Paint reaches the canvas only from piles you knife together on the
87: palette from the tubes in the box:
88: 
89: ```lua
90: p = pile{{"<tube>", <parts>}, {"<tube>", <parts>}}
91: q = pile{{"<tube>", <parts>}, medium=0.3}
92: print(p)                         -- pile(<tube> <parts>, <tube> <parts>; medium 0)
93: print(table.concat(tubes(), ", "))   -- the names in the box
94: ```
95: 
96: A pile is parts by volume of named tubes, plus `medium`: the share of oil
97: medium mixed in (0, as from the tube, to 0.95). Medium makes the paint more
98: transparent and more fluid, and slower to dry. It is added oil only. What a pile looks like is
99: what its pigments make together, thick or thin, over what is already on
100: the canvas; you find out by painting with it and looking. A pile mixed by
101: hand is a little uneven: each brushload takes slightly different
102: proportions (about 6%). The palette has room for 16 piles; the oldest is
103: scraped off to make room.
104: 
105: `turps` thins the pile with that share of turpentine (0 to 0.9):
106: `pile({{"<tube>", <parts>}, turps=0.6})`. It flows on the brush and
107: evaporates as the paint is laid, so it leaves a film that much thinner, of
108: the paint's own body: the lean, quick lay-in and wash. (`thinner`, below,
109: is the other way to thin a pile: its solvent stays in the film for a while
110: and leaves over painting time.) `oil` is what the paint is ground in: `"linseed"` (as the tubes come), `"walnut"` (dries a
111: little slower) or `"poppy"` (dries much slower, yellows least).
112: 
113: `blot` is the opposite of medium: the paint laid out on blotting paper
114: first, which draws out that share of its own oil (0 to 0.5):
115: `pile({{"<tube>", <parts>}, blot=0.3})`. Blotted paint is leaner, a little
116: more opaque and much stiffer: it holds the ridges and furrows of the brush
117: as it dries. A pile takes either medium or blot.
118: 
119: **The palette board.** Every pile is a heap on the board beside the easel.
120: 
121: - `pile{..., name="cool_mix"}` names it.
122: - `look --palette` (the `look` tool's `palette: true`) shows the board: each
123:   heap knifed out thick (its masstone and body) with a smear dragged from
124:   thick to thin across a black stripe (its tint as it thins, how much it
125:   hides), lit as in the gallery view. Judge a mix there before it touches the
126:   canvas.
127: - `p:add{{"<tube>", <parts>}, ..., medium=}` knifes more tube paint into a
128:   heap, in the units its recipe was given in (a pile knifed as
129:   `{"<tube A>", 4}, {"<tube B>", 0.35}` takes `{"<tube B>", 0.1}`
130:   as a tenth of a part more): look, adjust, look again. It returns the pile,
131:   its recipe with the added parts. The added paint is tube paint (linseed,
132:   unthinned), so it dilutes the heap's turpentine, its `thinner` and its oil;
133:   a scraped heap is knifed fresh first.
134: - `mix{{p1, <share>}, {p2, <share>}, ..., name=}` knifes heaps together into a
135:   new heap, as they are now.
136: - `palette{set_out={"<tube>", ...}}` sets out only those tubes, a limited
137:   palette: a pile of any other is an error.
138: - `palette{dirty=<0..1>}` keeps the board as dirty as painters do. A brush
139:   that comes to a heap carrying paint leaves a little of it there, more the
140:   fuller it is (a `b:reload` wipes it first), and the smears of the mixing
141:   area seep into each new heap, so the heaps drift toward each other through
142:   a sitting. `palette{clean=true}` scrapes the mixing area and skims the
143:   heaps. 0, the default, is a clean board: every heap stays as knifed.
144: - `palette()` returns a line about each heap: its recipe now, and how much of
145:   it is other paint.
146: 
147: The tube box:
148: 
149: | tube | pigment | hiding | stiffness | tinting strength | drying |
150: |---|---|---|---|---|---|
151: | lead white | basic lead carbonate | 0.82 | 0.8 | 1.0 | 2.0 |
152: | smalt | cobalt potash glass, coarse | 0.3 | 0.55 | 0.45 | 1.6 |
153: | pale smalt | a paler grade of smalt | 0.35 | 0.55 | 0.35 | 1.6 |
154: | yellow ochre | hydrated iron oxide earth | 0.8 | 0.7 | 0.8 | 0.8 |
155: | red earth | iron oxide earth | 0.85 | 0.7 | 0.9 | 1.0 |
156: | vermilion | mercuric sulfide | 0.9 | 0.75 | 1.0 | 0.4 |
157: | raw umber | iron and manganese oxide earth | 0.8 | 0.65 | 0.9 | 2.4 |
158: | bone black | charred bone (carbon, calcium phosphate) | 0.9 | 0.7 | 1.1 | 0.9 |
159: | cobalt blue | cobalt aluminate | 0.55 | 0.6 | 0.8 | 2.2 |
160: | chrome yellow | lead chromate | 0.9 | 0.7 | 1.0 | 1.8 |
161: | Prussian blue | iron ferrocyanide | 0.35 | 0.45 | 3.0 | 2.4 |
162: | green earth | celadonite and glauconite clay | 0.2 | 0.35 | 0.3 | 0.8 |
163: | Rinmann's green | cobalt-zinc oxide | 0.35 | 0.5 | 0.4 | 1.4 |
164: | copper green | verdigris ground in oil | 0.25 | 0.4 | 1.0 | 1.6 |
165: | Naples yellow | lead antimonate | 0.85 | 0.75 | 0.6 | 1.6 |
166: | rose madder | madder lake on alumina | 0.1 | 0.35 | 0.9 | 0.4 |
167: 
168: Hiding is how much one coat of the tube paint hides what is under it (0
169: transparent, 1 opaque). Stiffness is the paint's body as it comes from the
170: tube (0 fluid, 1 stiff). Tinting strength is relative to an average
171: pigment. Drying is the rate relative to average paint (higher dries
172: faster); a pile dries at its tubes' rates mixed by volume. These numbers
173: are estimates from the pigment literature.
174: 
175: ### Thinner
176: 
177: ```lua
178: w = pile{{"<tube>", <parts>}, thinner=0.5}          -- 0 (none) to 0.9
179: print(w)                         -- pile(<tube> <parts>; medium 0, thinner 0.5)
180: print(w.thinner)                 -- 0.5 (0.0 for a pile without it)
181: ```
182: 
183: `thinner` is the share of solvent (turpentine, spirits) by volume knifed
184: into the pile, 0 to 0.9. Medium is oil and stays in the film; the solvent
185: leaves it. With thinner, the pile's pigments, oil, body and drying rate
186: stay the paint's own.
187: 
188: What it does:
189: 
190: - A brushload of thinned paint is liquid, part paint and part solvent.
191:   One stroke of it lays only a thin film: each spot on the canvas takes
192:   at most a set thickness of liquid from one stroke, however many hairs
193:   or how many times the stroke passes over it. The more solvent, the
194:   thinner that film (about 6 µm at thinner 0.5). What the stroke can't
195:   lay stays in the brush, so a loaded brush goes a long way; another
196:   stroke over the same spot lays more.
197: - The solvent leaves over painting time, whether you wait or keep
198:   painting: in a thin film a few minutes, longer in a thicker one. The
199:   paint stays. Once it has gone, what is left is a thinner film
200:   of the paint itself, and more of what is under it shows through.
201: - While it is there the wet paint is more fluid: it levels and spreads a
202:   little, carrying its solvent with it. As the solvent goes, the paint
203:   firms up to its own body. The oil dries at its own rate all the while.
204: - Solvent has no color: the picture shows the paint alone.
205: - A brush or rag that lifts solvent-wet paint takes the solvent with it.
206: 
207: What it doesn't do (left out on purpose): the solvent doesn't evaporate
208: from the brush or the pile on the palette (a pile keeps its thinner), it
209: doesn't soak into the ground, and it doesn't dissolve paint that has set
210: or dried underneath. Solvent-wet paint comes up on a brush or rag no more
211: readily than the same paint without it. The thickness limits and the
212: evaporation times are estimates.
213: 
214: Thinner is new with this engine: a painting started on an older one
215: doesn't have it.
216: 
217: ## Brushes and strokes
218: 
219: ```lua
220: b = brush("filbert", 8)                  -- kinds: round, flat, filbert, fan, rigger, badger, stippler
221: b = brush{kind="round", width=3, point=1, stiffness=0.5}   -- also length, hair, run, lay, pickup,
222:                                                            -- push, splay, ragged, bristles
223: b:load(p, 0.8)                           -- dip into a pile: 0..1 of a full load
224: b:reload(q, 0.8)                         -- wipe most of the old paint off, then load
225: b:wipe(0.85)                             -- remove 85% of the paint onto the rag
226: b:fullness()                             -- paint left, 0..1
227: b:stroke({{120, 640}, {260, 470}, {430, 420}},
228:   {pressure={0.9, 0.3}, ramps={0.05, 0.4}, orient="across", shake=1, swell={1, 1.3, 0.8}, clip=m})
229: b:touch(400, 300, {pressure=0.6, drag={1, 0}, twist=0.2, angle=0.3, clip=m})
230: b:mark_width(0.4)                        -- the width of a mark at this pressure (units)
231: b:pressure_for(0.5)                      -- the pressure for a 0.5-unit line
232: ```
233: 
234: Widths are in canvas units. A brush keeps its paint across strokes and
235: chunks, so strokes from one load run dry, and a brush that has been
236: through wet paint carries some of it. Pressure ranges from 0 (lifted)
237: to 1 (fully pressed); a stroke's `pressure` takes a number for constant
238: pressure or `{start, end}`. A touch's `pressure` takes a number.
239: `ramps` gives the press-down and lift-off fractions, `swell` pressure factors
240: along the stroke, `orient` `"across"`, `"along"` or a fixed angle.
241: 
242: Brushes are blunt unless given a `point` (0 blunt, 1 a full point). A
243: pointed round or rigger lays a hairline at light pressure and spreads to
244: its belly when pressed, so its width follows the pressure and a stroke
245: whose pressure falls to 0 ends in a point.
246: 
247: **Loading part of the brush.** `b:load(p, amount, {side=, share=, streak=})`
248: dips only part of it: `side` (-1 or 1) and `share` (0..1) put one edge of
249: the brush in the pile (a double-loaded brush: two paints side by side in
250: one stroke), `streak` (0..1) takes it up unevenly in bands a few hairs
251: wide. In `work`, `streak=` does this on every dip and
252: `second={pile=, load=, side=, share=, streak=}` dips part of the brush in a
253: second pile after the first.
254: 
255: **Gestures.** `b:gesture({{x, y, p}, ...}, {wobble=, orient=, ramps=, shake=, clip=})` is one
256: deliberate stroke along a smooth curve through the points, its pressure
257: following each point's `p` (0..1; a point without one takes its
258: neighbors'): pressed hard at a root and lifted to nothing at a tip, swelling
259: through a turn. A pointed brush (`point=`) widens as it is pressed, so its
260: mark swells from a hairline and tapers back to one with the pressure; a
261: blunt one narrows at a light touch too (to about a third), but has no point.
262: `wobble` (units, up to 100) lets the hand drift sideways. Use gestures for the marks
263: that carry the picture: the few decisive strokes a passage needs.
264: 
265: **Thick paint.** `lay` (a brush option) sets how much paint a full brush
266: lays down: 1 for an ordinary load, 4 to 16 for impasto. Stiff paint
267: (blotted, or a stiff tube with no medium) holds what the brush leaves: in
268: it the hairs gather into clumps that lay the stroke in ridges and furrows
269: and push walls up along its edges, the coarser the hair (`hair`) the
270: coarser the clumps. Fluid paint levels out.
271: 
272: **The knife.** `k = knife{width=<units>}` is a painting knife, its blade
273: that long. `k:load(p, amount)` picks up paint, `k:wipe()` cleans it.
274: `k:lay(points, {pressure={a, b}, angle=, lift=})` drags it along the points
275: with the blade across the path (or at a fixed `angle`): it rests on the
276: surface's high points and stands off them by less the harder it is pressed,
277: filling what lies under it to the blade's level in a slab with a flat top,
278: or over dry impasto catching only the ridges; wet paint standing above the
279: blade is cut off into its bead or pressed out at its ends in ridges, and
280: the share `lift` of the bead (0.1) stays where it lifts.
281: `k:scrape(points, {pressure=, angle=, lift=})` scrapes wet paint off down
282: to the blade (at full pressure, down to the dry paint) and keeps it on the
283: blade, but for the share `lift` (0) it leaves where it lifts.
284: 
285: **Spatter.** `b:spatter{at={x, y}, toward={dx, dy}, spread=, force=, clip=}`
286: flicks the loaded brush: the paint its hairs can't hold flies off in droplets
287: toward `toward` (its length is how far the paint carries, in units), in a cone
288: `spread` radians either side (0.45 by default), `force` 0..1 hard (0.6). Fluid
289: paint (medium, turpentine) flies readily; blotted or stiff tube paint barely
290: leaves the brush. A hard flick throws many small droplets, a gentle one fewer
291: and bigger; heavier droplets carry farther, and those that land at a slant
292: stretch along their flight. Each comes off one hair with that hair's paint (a
293: double-loaded brush spatters both colors), and lands in the wet layer like
294: any paint. It returns how many droplets landed; `b:fullness()` shows what is
295: left on the brush.
296: 
297: ## Covering an area
298: 
299: ```lua
300: work(m, {hand="<hand>", pile=p, angle=<radians>, coverage=<layers>})
301: blend(m, {angle=<radians>})              -- a clean blender over wet paint (= work with hand="blend")
302: stipple(m, {pile=p, width=<units>, coverage=<layers>})
303: work(m, {hand="glaze", pile=q})          -- a thin layer brushed on with a soft brush
304: lose(m, {pile=p, where=0.5})
305: ```
306: 
307: `work` covers a mask with strokes of a real brush, planned the way a hand
308: lays them. `hand` picks a starting handling, which the options below
309: change:
310: 
311: | hand | tool | strokes |
312: |---|---|---|
313: | `broad` | filbert 22 | 80–220 units, bowing in long arcs, direction wandering over 350-unit patches |
314: | `body` (default) | filbert 9 | 20–60 units |
315: | `detail` | round 2.2 | 4–14 units, clipped to the mask |
316: | `hatch` | round 2.6 | 5–12 units, nearly straight, side by side, clumped |
317: | `glaze` | soft filbert 26 | 120–300 units, light pressure |
318: | `scumble` | filbert 9 | 10–20 units, worked back and forth |
319: | `blend` | badger 40 | a clean blender, crossing passes top to bottom, inside the mask. It is wiped clean as it goes, so it lifts paint as well as moving it: one pass takes up about 15% of a thin wet film, three passes about 40% |
320: 
321: | option | meaning |
322: |---|---|
323: | `pile` | the pile every stroke dips into (every hand but `blend`) |
324: | `tool` | `"filbert 8"`, `{kind=, width=, ...}` or a brush |
325: | `length` | `{min, max}` stroke length in units |
326: | `coverage` | layers of strokes over each point on average |
327: | `angle` | stroke direction: a number or `function(x, y)` |
328: | `pressure`, `ramps` | `{min, max}` pressure; attack and release fractions |
329: | `dips` | `{strokes per trip to the palette, load, wipe before dipping}` |
330: | `load`, `load_at` | load per dip; a number or `function(x, y)` that varies it |
331: | `edge` | how the passage meets the mask's edge (below) |
332: | `clip` | `true`: every bristle stops on the mask's edge; or a mask to clip to |
333: | `hug` | `true` (default): strokes reach the mask's edges; `false` lets coverage thin there |
334: | `piles` | graded color: `{{p1, w1}, {p2, w2}, ...}`, each weight a number or `function(x, y)`; each dip takes a mix of the piles by their weights at the stroke (the brush dipped into neighboring piles), so color changes continuously across one passage, with no seams between masks |
335: | `scale_at` | the size of the marks across the area: a number or `function(x, y)` multiplying stroke length and brush width (smaller where things are far, larger near); the pass lays more strokes where they are smaller, so its coverage holds |
336: | `fill` | `false` by default: gaps between strokes stay. Set `true` to follow the strokes with dabs into the gaps they left |
337: | `order` | `"passages"` (default), `"scatter"`, `"down"`, `"across"` or a sweep angle |
338: | `angle_jitter`, `curve` (`{bow, wave}`), `cross`, `drift` (`{amount, scale}`), `tail`, `broken`, `swell`, `clump`, `ruler` | how far the strokes depart from even ruler lines (`ruler=true` sets them straight and even) |
339: | `orient`, `shake`, `threshold`, `cut_in` (a tool), `scrub`, `blender`, `mix_jitter`, `seed` | the brush's orientation, the hand's unsteadiness, the mask level strokes are anchored at, cutting in the edge with a second tool, back-and-forth strokes, a clean brush, how uneven each dip of the pile is, the randomness |
340: 
341: Where an option takes `function(x, y)`, it is sampled every 2 units over
342: the area and interpolated. A mistyped option is an error that lists the
343: valid ones.
344: 
345: **What stays inside the mask.** `work` plans its strokes from the mask:
346: each stroke is anchored in it, but its path can begin outside and cross
347: the edge. By default `detail` and `blend` keep their paint inside the
348: mask. The other hands (`body`, `broad`, `hatch`, `glaze`, `scumble`) can
349: carry paint past the edge onto whatever is there, by as much as a stroke's
350: length (a `glaze` stroke is 120–300 units by default). `clip=true` keeps
351: every bristle inside the mask; `clip=` another mask keeps them inside that
352: one instead. `edge=` (below) shapes how the passage meets the edge, with
353: an overrun that varies and can reach beyond it.
354: 
355: **Edges.** `edge=` carries the passage up to the mask's edge the way a
356: brush does: each stroke stops by its own amount, and past the line its
357: film thins out over the weave. It takes a number from 0 (found: crisp) to
358: 1 (lost: the passage runs well past the line and dissolves), a name
359: (`"found"`, `"firm"`, `"soft"`, `"loose"`, `"lost"`), a function of
360: `(x, y)`, a mask, or a table: `{found=, soft=, lost=, period=40, seed=}`
361: lays those shares out along the contour in runs about `period` units long;
362: `waver=` and `reach=` scale how far the line wanders and how far strokes
363: run over. It can't be combined with `cut_in`.
364: 
365: **`stipple(m, {...})`** lays many small touches of a tip, each through the
366: bristles: `pile`, `width` (a stippler's width, 2 by default) or `tool`,
367: `coverage` (touches per point; a number or `function(x, y)`), `pressure`
368: `{min, max}`, `dips` `{touches per dip, load, wipe}`, `drag` (how far the
369: tip moves while down: a number or `{length, angle}`), `twist`, `cluster`
370: (0 even .. 1 in clumps, or `{amount, size}`), `feather` (0 by default;
371: above 0, touches get lighter where coverage is below 1), `clip`,
372: `mix_jitter`, `seed`.
373: 
374: **`lose(m, {pile=, where=, ...})`** drags a lightly loaded brush across
375: the mask's edge from the outside in, where `where` (as `edge=`; 1 by
376: default) is high: short strokes start outside, cross the edge at a slant
377: (or at `angle`) and lift off inside. Also `tool` (`"filbert 4"`), `reach`
378: (`{out, in}` units), `load` (0.2), `pressure` (`{0.35, 0.02}`), `every`
379: (a stroke every 1.2 brush widths), `seed`. It returns the number of
380: strokes.
381: 
382: `work`, `blend` and `stipple` also take `visible=`, `behind=`,
383: `at=` and `view=` (see [Depth](#depth)).
384: 
385: ## Masks and geometry
386: 
387: Masks are coverage maps (0..1) of the whole canvas. Operations return new
388: masks.
389: 
390: ```lua
391: everywhere()   rect(x, y, w, h)   ellipse(cx, cy, rx, ry)
392: poly({{x, y}, ...})   poly(pts, true)                  -- true: smoothed
393: below(function(x) return 150 + 0.6 * x end)   -- under a curve (or a point list)
394: above(curve)
395: ribbon(points, widths)   ribbon(points, 3)             -- a band along a line
396: mask(function(x, y) return x < 500 and 1 or 0 end)    -- any function, at every pixel
397: m + n   m * n   m - n   -m                             -- union, intersection, difference, inverse
398: m:roughen(units, period, seed, edge)   m:soften(units)   m:blur(units)
399: m:grow(units)   m:shrink(units)   m:offset(units)   m:rim(width, soft)
400: m:distance()   m:band(lo, hi, soft)   m:times(fn or mask)   m:map(function(v) return v * v end)
401: m:at(x, y)   m:area()
402: ```
403: 
404: Points are `{{x, y}, ...}` or a flat `{x1, y1, x2, y2, ...}`.
405: `below` selects larger y values, toward the bottom of the canvas;
406: `above` selects smaller y values, toward the top.
407: 
408: Numbers and randomness: `rand(a, b)`, `randn(mean, sd)`, `math.random`,
409: `lerp(a, b, t)`, `clamp(x, lo, hi)`, `smoothstep(a, b, x)`;
410: `noise{seed=, octaves=4, period=200, persistence=0.5, kind="fbm"|"ridged"|"billow", warp={period, amount, twice}, stretch={angle, k}}`
411: (call it as `n(x, y)` for about -1..1, `n:at01(x, y)` for 0..1; it can be
412: passed to `coverage=` or `load_at=`); `worley{seed=, period=, jitter=}`
413: (`c:at(x, y)` gives the distances to the nearest two cell points, how near
414: a cell wall, and a stable 0..1 per cell); `uneven(n, lo, hi, irregular,
415: clump, seed)` (n positions from lo to hi with uneven, clumped gaps).
416: 
417: The nested `warp` and `stretch` tables use positional values, not named
418: fields: for example, `noise{period=180, stretch={0, 3}}` stretches along
419: angle 0 by a factor of 3. `stretch={angle=0, k=3}` is not accepted.
420: 
421: **Drawn lines.** `outline{pts... or pts=, char=, seed=, closed=, open=,
422: corners=, corner_angle=60, size=, amount=, lobe=, edge=}` turns a few
423: points into a line drawn by hand (a smooth curve through them, broken at
424: corners marked `"c"`, with a hand's irregularity) and its mask:
425: 
426: ```lua
427: o = outline{{300, 600, "c"}, {320, 450}, {420, 380, "c"}, {560, 400}, {650, 480, "c"}, {500, 620}, char="firm", seed=3}
428: work(o:mask(), {hand="body", pile=p})
429: o:paint(b, {pressure=0.8, dip={p, 0.6}, every=3})   -- stroke the line itself
430: ```
431: 
432: | char | the line |
433: |---|---|
434: | `firm` (default for `outline`) | long strokes, slight overshoots, a crisp mask |
435: | `searching` | short strokes restated a little off each other, running past corners |
436: | `broken` | straight facets and chips in broken stretches between quiet ones |
437: | `soft` (default for `body_of`) | lobes of two sizes, light broken strokes, a mask edge lost in places |
438: 
439: `amount` scales the irregularity (0 is a clean curve), `lobe` sets the
440: lobe width in units, `edge` the mask's soft edge in units. An open line's
441: outside is on its left. `body_of{spine=, widths=, limbs={{pts..., widths=}, ...}, blend=0.8, char=}`
442: is the silhouette of a skeleton of points and widths. Methods: `o:mask()`,
443: `o:below(bottom)`, `o:above()`, `o:band(width, taper)`, `o:inset(d)`,
444: `o:offset(d)`, `o:paint(brush, {...})`, `o:path(i)`, `o:paths()`,
445: `o:strokes()`, `o:at(t)`, `o:length()`, `o:corners()`.
446: 
447: ## Drawing: pencil, chalk and eraser
448: 
449: ```lua
450: h = pencil("2H")                  -- or pencil{grade="2H"}: 9H..H, F, HB, B..9B
451: c = chalk()                       -- black chalk
452: h:sketch(pts, {pressure=0.3})     -- a few light passes (passes=3, wander= units, smooth=true)
453: h:line(pts, {pressure={0.5, 0.7, 0.4}})    -- one line through the points (smooth=false keeps corners)
454: h:rule({120, 700}, {860, 180}, {pressure=0.3})  -- straight, against a ruler
455: h:hatch(m, {angle=-1.1, pressure=0.35})         -- short parallel strokes (spacing=, length=)
456: h:width()   h.worn   h:sharpen()  -- the point blunts as you draw
457: erase(pts, {strength=0.9, width=9})  -- a kneaded eraser along a path, or erase(mask, {strength=})
458: fix()                                -- fixative (or fix(mask)): the eraser no longer lifts it
459: drawing_guide()                      -- the drawn lines themselves, as a continuous mask
460: ```
461: 
462: The point rides on the tops of the weave; pressure lets it reach into the
463: hollows. Soft leads lay darker, glossier lines, hard ones pale silver
464: lines. The eraser lifts most of a line, more from the tops than the
465: hollows, and leaves a ghost. Once paint has gone over the drawing it is
466: sealed: thin paint lets it show through, body paint hides it.
467: 
468: ## The rag
469: 
470: ```lua
471: r = rag()                                -- a clean cotton rag bunched into a pad, about 40 mm across
472: r = rag{width=<units>}
473: r:wipe(m, {pressure=0.5, angle=<radians>, passes=1, refold=<load>})   -- wiped over a mask
474: r:wipe(pts, {pressure={0.4, 0.8}})       -- one wipe along a path
475: r:blot(x, y, {pressure=0.6})             -- pressed straight down and lifted off
476: r:refold()                               -- a cleaner part of the cloth turned outward; retains dampness
477: r:dip(0.5)                               -- the part in use dipped into spirits, 0..1
478: print(r)                                 -- rag(width <units>, load <0..1>); also r.load, r.soaked, r.damp, r.fold
479: ```
480: 
481: A rag lifts open paint. The cloth rests on the tops of the weave and of
482: the paint, and reaches into the hollows as it is pressed harder
483: (`pressure` 0..1): paint comes off the tops first and stays longer in the
484: hollows. The last of a film comes away more and more slowly, so a dry rag
485: leaves a pale tint of the color that more wiping thins. Toward its rim the
486: pad presses lightly and reaches only the tops of the weave, so the edge of
487: a wipe shows the weave. Its folds and creases touch unevenly, so a wipe
488: leaves streaks along its path and a blot a crumpled patch. During a wipe,
489: a little freshly lifted paint smears back along the lightly pressed edges
490: and trailing end.
491: 
492: Fresh paint at the face's surface can smear into the next wipe too. It
493: gradually soaks into the cloth; refolding turns that paint inward.
494: 
495: A rag dipped in spirits (`r:dip`, 0..1) lifts wet paint more readily and
496: reaches farther into the hollows. It works gradually: wipe after wipe
497: takes the paint nearly to the ground. Its folds still leave streaks.
498: Dampness (`r.damp`) halves every three minutes of painting time. Refolding
499: retains the cloth's dampness; another dip adds spirits.
500: 
501: What it lifts soaks into the cloth. `r.load` is how loaded the part in use
502: is (0 clean, 1 full): the more loaded, the less it lifts. `r:refold()`
503: turns a cleaner part outward, though every part holds at least what has
504: soaked through the whole cloth (`r.soaked`, 0..1); `rag()` takes a fresh
505: one. These numbers can be read, not set. Over a mask, `refold=`
506: refolds whenever the load passes that value.
507: 
508: Over a mask, `wipe` lays wipes side by side across it in `angle`'s
509: direction, back and forth, each starting and stopping a little inside the
510: mask. The pad's rim reaches the mask's edge, and in places past it:
511: the rag isn't clipped to the mask. `passes` goes over it again, each time
512: a little turned. `seed=` fixes the cloth's folds.
513: 
514: **What it can't reach.** It lifts only open paint, and less the further
515: the paint has set: paint that is `"setting"` comes away slowly, and paint
516: past its gel point (`"tacky"` or `"dry"` under `drying(x, y)`) doesn't come
517: off at all. Paint laid over a set film lifts down to that film.
518: 
519: Hand time: a wipe takes the time to bring the pad down and drag it, at
520: about 150 mm a second; a blot about a second; a refold 3 seconds; a dip
521: 2.5 seconds; a fresh rag 5 seconds.
522: 
523: ## Solids, light and space
524: 
525: These are scaffolds for shapes you give them: they answer where light
526: and shadow fall and what lies in front of what.
527: 
528: **Form.** Solids in canvas units, z toward you, lit by one light:
529: 
530: ```lua
531: s = body.ellipsoid({400, 500, 0}, {120, 90, 80}):turn({400, 500, 0}, 0.3, 0.1, 0)
532:       :cut({400, 430, 0}, {-0.3, -1, 0.4}, 1, 3):rough(6, 120, 1)
533: k = body.block({650, 520, 0}, {160, 60, 90}, 3)       -- center, size, rounding
534: t = terrain{area={250, 200, 650, 500}, height=function(x, y) return 10 * math.sin(x / 60) end}
535: f = form{ {s, dist=0.3}, {k}, light={from={-1, -0.7}, front=0.5, ambient=0.2} }
536: f:value(x, y)   f:lit_at(x, y, soft)   f:part(x, y)   f:sample(x, y)   f:fall(x, y)   f:across(x, y)
537: f:lit{parts={1}, soft=0.12}   f:shadow{parts={1}}   f:silhouette{parts={1}}   f:edges{turn=0.8}   f:parts_mask{1}
538: work(f:lit{parts={1}}, {pile=p, angle=f:field("fall")})   -- field("fall"|"across"|"edge") for angle=
539: ```
540: 
541: Solids combine with `s:union(o)` and `s:subtract(o)`; `body.half_space(at,
542: normal)` cuts. The light also takes `bounce`, `bounce_from`, `penumbra`,
543: `reach`, `thickness` and `across_parts`.
544: 
545: **World (reference).** A space in meters seen in perspective: a camera
546: over a supporting surface, one directional light, and the bodies you
547: place there. Its calls:
548: 
549: ```lua
550: w = world{eye=<m>, fov=<degrees>}        -- camera height and field of view
551: s = w:spot(x, y)                         -- the surface seen at a canvas point (or w:spot_at(X, Z))
552: w, n = w:place(s, body.block(s:p(0, 0.5, 0), s:size(1, 1, 1), s:m(0.05)))   -- s:p, s:size, s:m: meters to units
553: v = w:view()                             -- trace once and keep it
554: v:bodies_mask{n}   v:shadows()   v:contact(0.25)   v:at(x, y)   v.form
555: w:to_ground(x, y)   w:project(X, Y, Z)   w:scale_at(Z)   w:height(x, y, meters)
556: w:shadow_angle(x, y)   w:sun_canvas()   w:ribbon(pts, width)   w:recede({X, Z}, {dX, dZ}, n)
557: ```
558: 
559: `world{}` options, all optional: `view` (the canvas rectangle it
560: covers), `horizon` (the canvas y of eye level), `eye`, `fov`, `ground` (a
561: function `(X, Z)` giving the surface's height in meters; flat by
562: default), `water` (`{level=, ripple=}`: a level reflecting surface),
563: `sun` (`{azimuth=, elevation=}` in degrees: the light's direction;
564: azimuth 0 is straight ahead, -90 to the left, 180 behind the eye),
565: `visibility` and `backdrop`. View queries: `v:water()` and `v:mirror(x,
566: y)` (with `water`), `v:land()` and `v:sky()` (where the surface and the
567: space above it are seen). `w:proxy(s, body)` places an unseen body that
568: casts a shadow. `w:aerial(Z)` and `aerial(dist, visibility)` give
569: how much air lies between the eye and a distance (0..1).
570: 
571: **Depth.** A view knows what lies behind what. `w = w:layer(name, mask,
572: depth)` registers a shape you paint by hand at a depth (meters, a spot, a
573: canvas point `{x, y}` where it stands on the ground, or `"ground"`); make
574: the view after it. Then `v:visible(x)`, `v:front(x)`, `v:behind(x)`,
575: `v:at_depth(m)`, `v:between(a, b)` and `v:seen(x, y)` are masks and
576: answers, and `v:cast_shadow{soft=, from=}` and `v:contact_shadow{reach=,
577: from=}` are shadows that fall off with distance from what casts them.
578: Things are named by body number, layer name, `"ground"`, `"water"`,
579: `"surface"`, `"sky"`, `"bodies"`, `"layers"`, a mask or a list. Passes take
580: `visible=` (only where that is seen), `behind=` (only where nothing in
581: front of it is) and `at=` (a depth in meters): strokes still overrun the
582: mask's own edges and stop at what is in front.
583: 
584: ## Time
585: 
586: Painting takes time, and paint dries on the painting's clock. Only
587: painting operations (strokes, touches, passes, trips to the palette) and
588: `wait(minutes)` advance it. Real time between chunks does not: paint
589: doesn't dry while you think. `wait(minutes)` passes that much painting
590: time at once.
591: 
592: Every successful paint reply reports the current painting time, before
593: `ok`.
594: 
595: - **Hand time.** Every stroke, touch, pass and trip to the palette takes
596:   the time a hand takes to make it: a stroke by its length and the
597:   brush's width (broad sweeps are fast, fine lines slow per mm), a
598:   stipple touch about a third of a second, a dip into a pile on the
599:   palette 2.5 s, knifing a new pile 20 s. The paint ages while the hand
600:   works: a long pass is painted in slices of 15 minutes, and its first
601:   strokes are setting by the time the last go on.
602: - **`wait(minutes)`** lets time pass with your hand away from the canvas:
603:   minutes, hours or days (`wait(3 * 24 * 60)`), up to 10 years
604:   (5,259,600 minutes). It returns the time of day, e.g. `day 3, 14:20`
605:   (the painting was begun at 09:00 on day 1).
606: - **`drying(x, y)`** tells you what the paint there is like to the touch:
607:   `"open"` (workable: it blends and lifts), `"setting"` (stiff, barely
608:   blends), `"tacky"` (set; it grabs the brush) or `"dry"` (touch-dry).
609:   It reads the top film at that point: where no wet paint lies there (a
610:   gap between strokes, a wiped spot), it reads the layer beneath.
611: 
612: Each film dries at its own pace, set by its pigments, its thickness and
613: its oil. It is open for the first 30% of its time to touch-dry, setting
614: until 60%, then tacky until it is touch-dry. A stroke of lead white or raw
615: umber from a loaded broad brush is open for 12 to 14 hours, tacky after
616: about a day and touch-dry in under two days. Cobalt blue, Prussian blue
617: and burnt sienna are about as fast. Raw sienna, ochres, earths, cadmiums,
618: ultramarine and bone black are touch-dry in 3½ to 5 days, madder in about 11.
619: Thinner paint dries sooner and thicker paint later: twice a stroke's
620: thickness takes 1.6 times as long. Thick, oily paint of slow pigments can stay open for weeks. Wet paint
621: under a new stroke comes up into it; paint laid over dry paint sits on
622: top of it.
623: 
624: ## Looking
625: 
626: `look` shows you the canvas as it is now, with wet paint as laid. A whole
627: view shows all of it, scaled down, like stepping back. A crop shows the
628: canvas at its full detail, 2.4 pixels to a canvas unit, and may be at most
629: 500 units on either side. `crop: "x0,y0,x1,y1"` gives two opposite corners
630: in canvas units, not a position and width/height.
631: 
632: | `look` with | shows |
633: |---|---|
634: | nothing | the whole canvas, scaled down |
635: | `crop: "300,200,500,350"` | a window in canvas units, at full detail |
636: | `mode: "value"` | in grays |
637: | `mode: "squint"` | blurred, as through half-closed eyes |
638: | `mode: "mirror"` | flipped left to right |
639: | `mode: "relief"` | under a raking light from the upper left, so the paint's ridges, furrows and slabs show (wet paint shines) |
640: | `mode: "gallery"` | as the picture hangs: lit from above and a little left at 55°, so impasto models softly |
641: | `mode: "relief"`, `light: "45,15"` | the light from that azimuth (degrees: 0 from the right, 90 from the top) and elevation; the lower the light, the harsher |
642: | `mode: "value,squint"`, `size: 600` | modes combine; `size` sets the long side |
643: | `grid: true` | a squared grid in canvas units, labeled along the edges |
644: | `crop: "300,200,500,350"`, `grid: 10` | a window with a grid every 10 units |
645: 
646: The grid is drawn on the PNG only, like the squares ruled over a drawing
647: to transfer it.
648: 
649: `look` with `palette: true` shows the palette board instead of the canvas:
650: each live heap's masstone and body paint, with a smear dragged across a
651: black stripe. It shows the heap's paint before the unevenness of a
652: brushload. It takes no
653: other option, and nothing on the canvas or the clock changes.
654: 
655: | `look` with | shows |
656: |---|---|
657: | `survey: true` | the whole canvas at full detail, as several tiles of at most 500 units (2 × 2 for most canvases, 2 × 1 for one twice as wide as high), each a separate image; modes apply (`mode: "gallery"`) |
658: | `compare: "<an earlier look's path>"` | that earlier image on the left and the current view on the right, at the same height. The right is the view the other options ask for (`size: 800` without `crop` or `size`); the earlier picture is only resized to its height, so repeat the earlier look's crop, modes, light and grid options to compare the same view |
659: | `hold: "<a knife's or a pile's name>"`, `at: "x,y"` | (speculative) the loaded knife held up to the canvas: the passage around the point (240 units square, clipped at the canvas's edges, or your `crop`) with the blade's end at it, the paint thick on the steel, seen in the same light and mode as the passage (`mode` value, squint, relief or gallery, and `light`; not mirror, `grid`, `size`, `palette`, `survey` or `compare`). A knife shows what is on it, as full as it is up to a full load; a pile, a fresh full load. It shows the paint on the knife, not how it would look laid |
660: 
661: A survey can arrive in a partial batch to fit the painter's image budget.
662: The reply lists the remaining tile paths; read them one at a time to inspect
663: the rest of the canvas.
664: 
665: A whole view defaults to 1000 pixels on its long side (`size` up to 1600),
666: about 42% of a 2400-pixel canvas's width: small marks, beads of paint and
667: stray strokes can be hard to see in it. Survey the canvas after
668: each campaign, and compare before and after.

670: ## How chunks behave
671: 
672: - **Option types.** Each option takes the type shown in this guide.
673:   Options documented as `function(x, y)` accept a Lua function; numeric
674:   options take the computed number.
675: - **Globals persist, locals don't.** Each chunk is its own Lua chunk:
676:   `p = pile{...}` is there in later chunks, `local p = ...` is not.
677: - **Randomness is deterministic.** `math.random`, `rand` and `randn` are
678:   reseeded at the start of every chunk from the canvas's seed and the
679:   chunk's number, and passes pick their own seeds the same way (pass
680:   `seed=` to fix one). A replay paints the same thing, and a failed chunk
681:   doesn't shift the next one's randomness.
682: - **No OS access.** `io`, `os`, `debug`, `require`, `dofile`, `loadfile`

687:   declarations (one switches its chunk to strict mode). There is no
688:   `math.atan2`: `math.atan(y, x)` takes two arguments. `%d` in

692: - **`pairs` walks a table in the same order in every session and replay.**
693:   Every table walks in a fixed order: booleans, numbers, strings (each
694:   ascending), then other keys in the order they were made. (Paintings

699:   in `print`, `tostring`, `string.format`'s `%s` and errors alike, and
700:   `%p` is refused: an address differs from run to run, so a replay would
701:   print or choose differently.
702: - **Memory.** Masks and forms are large: keep big ones `local` when

704: 
705: ## The scratch canvas
706: 
707: Beside the painting stands a scratch canvas for trying out a mix, a stroke, a glaze or a
708: drying time before it goes on the painting. `paint`, `look`, `status` and `log` work on it
709: with `scratch: true`; without it they work on the painting.
710: 
711: - The first chunk painted on it sets it up as the painting's canvas was set up: the same
712:   size, linen and ground. The painting needs its own `canvas{}` first.
713: - It is a separate canvas: its own palette, brushes, knives, rags and variables (a pile
714:   knifed for the painting has to be knifed again here), and its own log,
715:   `paintings/lua/scratch.lua`. Nothing done on it reaches the painting.
716: - It keeps its own clock. Time spent or waited there (`wait`, `dry()`, `glaze()`) doesn't

718: - To use what worked, paint it on the painting: the same pile, the same handling.
719: - `new_scratch: true` (with `scratch: true`) puts the scratch canvas aside and starts a

721: - A trial judges a passage only as far as it repeats that passage's conditions: lay the
722:   underlayer you mean to work over, and let it dry as long as it has on the painting.
723: 
724: ## Color, planes and open coverage
725: 
726: These tools build a picture from color and separately drawn planes,
727: alongside the lit-volume and perspective scaffolds above. The subject,
728: canvas and arrangement are yours:
729: 
730: | Idea | Tools and parameters |
731: |---|---|
732: | Color-built space | Related warm/cool `pile{}` mixtures; separate `b:stroke` marks, or `work` with weighted `piles`. Relative warmth can advance and coolness recede; check the effect with a laid trial. |
733: | Compressed depth and tilted planes | Separately drawn `poly` masks and stroke paths; adjust spacing, tilt, overlap and relative color intensity. A `world{}` projection is optional. |
734: | Volumes and facets | Plane divisions drawn with `poly` or brush paths, related through color; `form{}` is optional, as a volume guide. |

737: | Multiple viewpoints | Separately drawn plane masks and paths can each take their own orientation; `look` checks how they relate across the whole picture. |
738: 
739: ## The journal
740: 
741: `notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `note` appends an entry
742: stamped with the painting's time, such as `day 2, 09:40`. To revise what
743: is already there, call `note` with `replaces`, the exact passage to
744: change, and `text`, what takes its place. Writing a note doesn't advance

1: # Techniques at the easel
2: 
3: How the oil painter's techniques are done with this easel's tools, and the
4: traps that cost a painting time. `notes/easel_guide.md` says what each tool
5: does; this says how to use them. What you paint is yours to choose.
6: 
7: ## Plan before you paint
8: 
9: - **Try it on the scratch canvas** (`scratch: true`): a mix, a stroke, a
10:   glaze, a wipe. Lay the underlayer it will go over, let it dry as long as
11:   it has on the painting, and compare the trial with the passage in a detail
12:   crop. Then paint it on the painting with the same pile and the same
13:   handling.
14: - **Plan in values.** `look` with `mode: "value,squint"` shows the picture as
15:   big masses of light and dark. Make the masses hold there before you add
16:   detail.
17: - **Coordinates.** A look's pixels are not canvas units. Use `grid: true` (or
18:   a crop with `grid: 10`) to read positions off a look before you aim a mask
19:   at something you saw.
20: 
21: ## Before another pass: a decision checklist
22: 
23: 1. **Check the paint state.** Use `drying(x, y)` along the next pass and
24:    at its edges: `"open"` blends and lifts; `"setting"` is stiff and barely
25:    blends; `"tacky"` has set and grabs the brush; `"dry"` is touch-dry.
26:    The call reads the top film. Where no wet paint lies, as in a gap
27:    between strokes, it reads the set layer beneath. A set layer under wet
28:    paint can still be tacky and grab the brush, so read a nearby gap too.
29:    Lay into open paint when you want strokes to fuse; wait for it to set
30:    when you want them separate. If tacky paint breaks the stroke, wait
31:    longer. See the guide's [Time](easel_guide.md#time).
32: 2. **Diagnose a failed deposit in a detail crop.** Check the load, the
33:    paint the brush passed through and the layer beneath.
34:    - Gaps between marks: if the brush runs dry, use shorter strokes and
35:      reload more often. If gaps remain, check brush contact and coverage;
36:      extra coverage can add dabs and relief.
37:    - A continuous thin film showing the undercolor: test less thinning,
38:      a fuller deposit or a mixture with stronger hiding. Evidence for
39:      these fixes is limited, so compare them on the scratch canvas first.
40:    - A mixture changed by paint carried on the brush: use a fresh brush.
41:      If open underpaint caused the pickup and you want separate color,
42:      wait for it to set. Check the pile itself before changing its recipe.
43: 3. **Prepare a transition.** Mix a few in-between tones, lay them and
44:    look. Blend while the paint is open, as [Blending](#blending) describes,
45:    and stop at the signs listed there. In dry paint, build the transition
46:    with new paint.
47: 4. **Choose a repair.** If further handling keeps mixing an unsuccessful
48:    wet deposit, scrape or lift it before restating it. The knife scrapes
49:    wet paint down to set paint; the rag lifts and smears it and leaves a
50:    trace. Inspect what remains before repainting. See
51:    [The knife](#the-knife) and [The rag](#the-rag) for handling and limits.
52: 5. **Test a doubtful change.** Use the scratch procedure in
53:    [Plan before you paint](#plan-before-you-paint), matching the underpaint
54:    and its drying state. Change one condition, compare the results and
55:    carry the handling that worked over to the painting. Leave the passage
56:    alone if another pass has no clear benefit.
57: 
58: ## Ground
59: 
60: - An **oil ground** (the default) absorbs nothing: paint stays open and
61:   glossy longer. An **absorbent ground** (`absorbent=true`) drinks the oil of
62:   thin paint: matte, lean, quick to set, colors that sit on the surface;
63:   thick paint is barely touched. Choose before you start: it is the
64:   canvas's character.
65: - A **toned ground** (a little ochre, umber or black in the white) sets the
66:   middle value from the first stroke; a white ground keeps everything high
67:   in key and lets thin paint glow.
68: 
69: ## Lay-in: lean, quick, thin
70: 
71: - Thin the paint with turpentine (`pile{..., turps=0.6}`) for the first
72:   drawing and masses: it flows, covers fast and leaves a thin film that
73:   dries before the next sitting.
74: - **Fat over lean.** Each layer should be at least as oily as the one under
75:   it: lay-in lean (turpentine, blotted), body as from the tube, glazes rich
76:   (medium). Lean over fat dries matte and patchy over a still-soft layer.
77: 
78: ## The whole picture, every time
79: 
80: - **Step back after every campaign** and ask whether the whole picture still
81:   does what you meant it to, as well as whether the last thing you fixed is
82:   fixed. Then `survey` it at full detail: what you can't see in a whole view
83:   is still on the canvas.
84: - **Values.** Check `mode: "value,squint"`: do the large lights, middles
85:   and darks give the effect you want? Light reads against darks; a high-key
86:   picture can keep a narrow range on purpose.
87: - **Light relationships.** Relate the light and shadow of each passage to
88:   the effect you want. A uniform band or a firm boundary can serve the
89:   picture; judge it against the whole.
90: - **Forms meet through relationships.** Overlap, color and edge handling
91:   separate or connect adjacent planes. A boundary that is only a mask's
92:   edge leaves their spatial relationship unstated.
93: - **Composition**: judge how the masses work together for the effect you
94:   chose. Where the emphasis sits, central or off-center, is yours to
95:   choose.
96: 
97: ## Marks
98: 
99: - **A hierarchy of marks.** A few large decisive strokes (`b:gesture`), many
100:   middle ones, some small accents. One stroke size and one shape over a whole
101:   area reads as texture.
102: - **Mark scale and distance.** Marks that shrink through a passage
103:   (`scale_at`) can suggest recession; marks of similar scale throughout
104:   can compress depth.
105: - **Mark direction and form.** Direction can turn with a plane or bind
106:   neighboring planes through a shared rhythm. Strokes that wander in
107:   every direction read as noise.
108: - **Light and texture.** Bright light reads as light with soft edges and
109:   little texture. Busy or outlined strokes inside it, or strokes circling
110:   a center, turn it into an object.
111: 
112: ## Spatter
113: 
114: - **Flicked paint makes scattered marks.**
115:   `b:spatter{at={x, y}, toward={dx, dy}}` throws droplets whose sizes,
116:   spacing and colors vary by themselves: aim the flick and let the droplets
117:   fall.
118: - **Thin the paint to make it fly**: a pile with medium or turpentine
119:   spatters; blotted paint hardly does. A hard flick gives a fine spray, a
120:   gentle one fat drops.
121: - **Mask what must stay clean** with `clip=`: droplets fly past any edge.
122: - A few flicks over a passage, then look.
123: 
124: ## Forms and shadows
125: 
126: - **A form can read as one mass.** Relate its parts through color and
127:   overlap so they hold together. `form{}` gives a lit-volume guide, and
128:   color modulation builds solidity with or without that lighting.
129: - **Shadows take color from surrounding light.** With warm light reflected
130:   up near its base and cooler light from above, a shadow is warmer near its
131:   base and cooler above. Grade it in separate passes with different `pile=`
132:   values, and judge its value and temperature against the object casting
133:   it and the passages around it. One violet for every shadow is the usual
134:   trap.
135: - **Distance and color.** Distance lightens and cools: far forms are paler
136:   and bluer than near ones and closer to each other in tone. Similar
137:   intensity in near and far planes can compress depth.
138: 
139: ## The palette
140: 
141: - **Look at the board before the canvas.** `look` with `palette: true` shows
142:   each heap thick and thinned over black: a chalky mix, a violet "gray", a
143:   glaze that stains or one that hides show there, before they cost a passage.
144: - **Steer a mix by eye**: `p:add{}` a touch at a time, looking between
145:   additions.
146: - **Matching a passage** for a repair: start from its recipe in the log and
147:   lay a trial beside it. The layers since may have shifted the passage, so
148:   judge the laid trial in a detail crop.
149: - **Set out a limited palette** for a picture that should hang together; a
150:   few tubes mixed every way give related colors by themselves.
151: - **A dirty board unifies.** `palette{dirty=0.2}` to `0.4` lets each heap
152:   pick up a trace of the others through a sitting, as a working palette does;
153:   clean it (`palette{clean=true}`) when a passage needs pure color.
154: 
155: ## Broken color
156: 
157: - **Many close piles.** Knife three to five piles of neighboring colors
158:   (warmer, cooler, lighter, darker) and lay them as separate strokes over
159:   the same area; the eye mixes them. `mix_jitter=` in `work` varies each
160:   dip; every pile is a little uneven.
161: - **Two colors on one brush.** `b:load(p, 0.8); b:load(p2, 0.5, {side=1, share=0.4})`, or
162:   `work(m, {pile=p, second={pile=p2, side=1, share=0.45}})`: each stroke carries both,
163:   side by side, mingling as it goes. `streak=` loads unevenly, in bands.
164: - **Wet into wet.** A stroke dragged through wet paint picks some of it up
165:   and carries it along: color changes within the stroke. Work an area while
166:   it is open (`drying(x, y)` says "open") for soft transitions; wait for it
167:   to set for crisp, separate strokes on top.
168: - **Watch the white.** Every pile with much lead white is chalky. Keep white
169:   for the lights; let the darks and middles be pigment.
170: - **Corrections stay close in value.** Keep a correction within a value step
171:   of what surrounds it, and small accents near their surroundings' value: a
172:   thin pale accent against a dark reads as a crack.
173: - **Vary the touch.** One stroke length and one brush over a whole canvas
174:   reads as a mechanical texture. Change brush size, stroke length, direction
175:   and pressure from passage to passage; leave some passages quiet.
176: 
177: ## Impasto
178: 
179: - **Thick paint for lights and accents.** Most of a canvas is thin: lay-in and shadows
180:   lean (turpentine), middle tones as from the tube. Keep the thick, blotted
181:   paint for the lights and the accents. Impasto everywhere reads as flat.
182:   `load_at=` varies the load across a pass; `scale_at` gives ridges of
183:   different sizes.
184: 
185: - Stiff paint holds the brush's marks: blot it (`pile{..., blot=0.3}`) or
186:   use it as it comes from the tube, with no medium. A full brush lays more with `lay=4`
187:   to `lay=16`; a coarse hog brush (larger `hair`) leaves coarser ridges.
188: - In stiff paint the hairs gather into clumps: strokes lie in ridges and
189:   furrows, walls rise along their sides, a bead where they end. Fluid paint
190:   levels flat, which suits a glaze.
191: - Check it with `look` and `mode: "relief"` (raking light from the upper
192:   left at 25°: it exaggerates, as a raking lamp does) and with
193:   `mode: "gallery"` (55°, as the picture is seen on a wall). Judge the
194:   picture under the gallery light; use raking light to inspect the surface.
195: - Let impasto set before painting into it, unless you want the new stroke
196:   to drag the old one along.
197: 
198: ## The knife
199: 
200: - `k = knife{width=30}; k:load(p, 1.0); k:lay(points, {pressure={0.5, 0.5}})`
201:   lays a slab with a flat top, torn where it parts from the blade (its ends,
202:   its leading edge): light pressure lays it thick, and the paint runs out
203:   sooner; firm pressure thin, and it goes further. The points set its path.
204: - Pulled lightly over **dry** impasto, it catches only the ridges: broken
205:   color over a textured underlayer, a sparkle of light paint on dark.
206: - `k:scrape(points, {pressure=1})` takes wet paint off down to what is dry:
207:   to restate a passage, or to leave a ghost of it.
208: 
209: ## Blending
210: 
211: - **Blend inside one passage.** Shape the mask like the passage, with its
212:   edge where the paint already matches. Keep everything you want to keep
213:   outside the mask, dry shapes included: the blender carries wet paint onto
214:   them.
215: - **Look after each pass.** The blender lifts paint as it moves it. When
216:   darks go pale, texture flattens or the weave shows through, stop.
217: - **A seam that keeps coming back** needs another method. A smaller patch
218:   blended again rebuilds the box. Try something else across the whole
219:   transition on the scratch canvas: a thin tint of the original recipe,
220:   interlocking strokes of the two neighboring colors over dry paint, or the
221:   connected passage repainted up to its natural edges.
222: 
223: ## Glazing and scumbling (over dry paint)
224: 
225: - **Glaze**: a transparent paint (lakes, viridian, ultramarine, a little of
226:   anything) with plenty of medium (0.7 to 0.85), `hand="glaze"`, over a dry
227:   passage. It deepens and saturates and lets the light underneath through;
228:   it rescues a chalky passage. Over impasto it pools in the valleys and
229:   thins on the ridges, which then shine through. Too much pigment, or any
230:   white, lays an opaque veil: try it small first. A glaze over the whole
231:   picture to pull it together has failed more often than it has worked.
232: - **Scumble**: light paint dragged thin over a dry darker passage, broken
233:   by the surface. A light load and
234:   `hand="scumble"` often lay opaque dabs. The veils that blended in came
235:   from paint thinned with `thinner`, laid in several light passes. Try it
236:   on the scratch canvas first.
237: - Glazes and scumbles want the passage under them **dry** (`wait` until
238:   `drying` says so): over open paint they just mix.
239: 
240: ## Keeping control
241: 
242: - **Clip** a pass near anything it must not touch (`clip=` a mask). The body
243:   hands carry paint past their mask's edge by as much as a stroke's length:
244:   without a clip they paint over what is next to them.
245: - **Protect what is there now.** Paint fine marks after the passages behind
246:   them where you can. In every later pass over that area, subtract each of
247:   them from the mask (`m - protected`), and subtract again after `grow` or
248:   `blur`, which spread the mask back over them.
249: - **Check a mask before painting through it**: `print(m:at(x, y))` at a few
250:   points inside the target and just outside it, past each end of a band.
251: - **Masks from earlier chunks**: a `local` mask is gone in the next chunk.
252:   Keep what later chunks need as globals: paths, recipes, protection masks.
253:   Before redrawing something by eye, look for its saved path. Keep big
254:   temporary masks local (memory).
255: - **Small forms** drawn as a neat diagram of separate parts can read as
256:   icons. A few thick, irregular touches of two or three colors read as the
257:   thing.
258: - **Taking paint off**: wet paint comes off with the rag (below) or the
259:   knife, down to the first set layer. Set paint stays: paint over it or
260:   glaze it. Either way it costs only painted time.
261: 
262: ## The rag
263: 
264: - **It lifts wet paint down to the first set layer.** Earlier passes that
265:   haven't set are part of the same wet film, so a firm lift can take them
266:   too, down to set paint or the ground. Before a wipe, check
267:   `drying(x, y)` in the paint: `"open"` paint lifts, `"setting"` paint
268:   comes away slowly, and `"tacky"` or `"dry"` paint has set and stays.
269:   A wipe usually leaves a thin wet tint, and `drying(x, y)` reads that
270:   tint as `"open"` or `"setting"`. If the tint is `"setting"`, or the set
271:   layer under it is still tacky, it grabs the brush when you repaint.
272:   Check it at a nearby gap in the paint, where `drying(x, y)` reads the
273:   set layer.
274: - **Dip it for a lift.** A dry rag mostly moves paint and leaves its color
275:   in the weave: useful for wiping lights out of a wet glaze or lay-in. To
276:   take a passage off, dip well (`r:dip(0.9)`), press firmly, give it two or
277:   three passes, then go over it again across the first direction with a
278:   fresh, dipped rag.
279: - **The spirits go in minutes.** Dampness halves every three minutes of
280:   painting time, and a long mask wipe takes minutes. Dip just before each
281:   wipe; `print(r.damp)` says how much is left.
282: - **A loaded face puts paint back.** `print(r.load)`: near 1, the face
283:   lifts little and smears. Refold (`refold=` in a mask wipe) or take a
284:   fresh rag.
285: - **The rag runs past the mask.** Its rim reaches past the mask's edge and
286:   lays lifted paint on what is next to it, dry shapes included. Keep the
287:   mask clear of edges you need crisp. Along an edge, wipe a path parallel
288:   to it with a rag narrower than the strip.
289: - **Shape the mask like the passage.** Mask wipes start and stop a little
290:   inside the mask, so a rectangle leaves a frame of the wiped color. If a
291:   frame shows, wipe along its sides with a path.
292: - **Expect a trace.** Even a good lift leaves a tint, streaks along the
293:   wipe or a rim where it stopped. Look at a detail crop before you call it
294:   clean, and before you paint over it. Thick paint takes many fresh, dipped
295:   wipes.
296: - **One lift, then a new plan.** If the same passage needs lifting twice,
297:   change what goes on it before painting it again.
298: 
299: ## Time
300: 
301: - Time passes only as you paint or `wait`. Paint dries on its own clock:
302:   lead white and umber fast, lakes and vermilion slow, thin paint faster than
303:   thick. Added medium and the slower oils (walnut, poppy) slow it; an
304:   absorbent ground sets thin paint laid straight on it quickly.
305: - **Check `drying(x, y)` at several points** along the next pass, its edges
306:   included: thick and thin parts of one passage dry at different rates.
307: - A painting can take months of painted time. Let layers dry between
308:   campaigns; that is what lets the next one sit on top.
309: 
310: ## Finishing
311: 
312: - An unvarnished picture keeps its matte and glossy passages as painted.
313:   A varnish (where the easel has one) makes it all glossy: darks deepen.

3: Observations of the canvas, the paint and the tools at this easel, by

9: ## The canvas and ground
10: 
11: 1. The linen's vertical threads are more even than the horizontal ones,
12:    which carry thick slubs a few millimeters long; their spacing follows the
13:    counts set in `canvas{}`.
14: 2. The ground chosen in `canvas{}` shows through thin paint; body color
15:    hides it.
16: 3. Light paint laid at light pressure over a wet dark catches only the high
17:    points of a knife-textured ground. The dark stays in the hollows as a
18:    net of fine dark lines that looks like cracking.
19: 4. Bristles plow paint off the tops of the weave, so a lay-in can keep
20:    small specks of bare ground. A denser pass covers them.
21: 
22: ## Paint in thin films
23: 
24: 5. A coat of paint over paint of its own masstone looks the same at any
25:    thickness, so a mark from a pile matching what it lies on disappears
26:    into it.
27: 6. A thin film looks different from its pile. Thin dark or earth mixtures over
28:    a pale passage come out lighter, warmer and more saturated than the
29:    masstone on the palette.
30: 7. The thin fringe of an umber or black stroke over a light field dries
31:    as a warm brown to warm gray halo. A blue stroke's fringe stays blue.
32: 8. Lead white hides strongly (its hiding in the guide's tube table is
33:    0.82; how much a coat covers also depends on its thickness). A thin veil
34:    of a pale lead-white mixture lies over what is under it and lightens it,
35:    like a scumble.
36: 
37: ## Brushes
38: 
39: 9. Every brush is blunt unless given a `point`. A blunt brush's mark runs
40:    from about half its width at the lightest touch to its full width pressed
41:    (a little more with splay), so it can't taper to a point.
42: 10. A pointed brush at light pressure lays a hairline, and its width grows
43:     with pressure. A band a few units wide needs real pressure or a blunt
44:     brush of that width. A stroke whose pressure falls off at the end draws
45:     down to the tip and still reaches the end of its path.
46: 11. A brush keeps its paint across strokes. Each stroke lays most at its
47:     start, and the load runs down along the stroke, so a long drag with a
48:     wide brush runs dry partway and leaves thinly covered streaks and bands.
49: 12. A well-loaded hair wets the hollows of the weave. A nearly empty one
50:     skims the tops (dry brush, broken color). Soft hair bends down into the
51:     hollows; stiff bristle rides on the tops.
52: 13. Whether a dry brush breaks up depends on its load, the pressure, the
53:     paint below and the ground's texture.
54: 14. A pointed brush loaded below about a quarter stops wetting the hollows,
55:     and its thin line breaks up along the weave. Run dry, the tip loses its
56:     point and splits.
57: 15. A pressed touch lays one continuous, nearly round patch (the paint
58:     bridges the hairs) that grows with pressure.

60: ## Strokes, passes and clipping
61: 
62: 16. `clip=true` stops every bristle on the mask's edge, weighted by the
63:     mask's value. A clipped fill reproduces the mask's outline exactly, as
64:     one even line, steps and corners included. The `detail` and `blend`
65:     hands are clipped by default; `broad`, `body`, `hatch`, `glaze` and
66:     `scumble` are unclipped.
67: 17. Unclipped strokes run past the mask's edge by their own length and
68:     width. Along a long straight edge they throw small irregular patches into the field
69:     beyond, and a brush wider than a band spreads well outside it.
70: 18. The square ends of unclipped strokes notch a shape's edge into steps.
71: 19. In `work`, the mask's value decides where strokes are anchored (at or
72:     above `threshold`: 0.3, or 0.1 for `detail`). Unclipped, strokes end
73:     where their lengths end, however soft the mask's edge.
74: 20. `work` leaves the ground showing between its strokes. With `fill=true`
75:     it looks at its passage afterward and dabs paint into the bare spots its
76:     strokes left. Single `stroke` and `touch` calls don't fill in.
77: 21. Short strokes planned along a band about one unit wide come out as a
78:     dashed line: the planner lays them separately, with gaps.
79: 22. Parallel strokes that all break at the same places leave a row of stroke
80:     ends across the passage, and the outer strokes' ends make a lobed edge.
81: 23. `cut_in` with a round along a curved edge lays short strokes that follow
82:     it as a string of small bumps.
83: 24. In a smooth lean passage, the loaded starts of broad strokes stay as
84:     lighter patches. Blending reduces them and leaves traces.
85: 
86: ## Wet into wet
87: 
88: 25. A brush over open paint lifts some of it and mixes it with its own. A
89:     clean brush lifts wet paint, less as it sets, and nothing from set or
90:     dry paint.
91: 26. Light touches into a wet dark dissolve into it. The same touches on
92:     paint that has set stay where they land.
93: 27. A pale stroke dragged through a wet dark picks up the dark and comes out
94:     streaked, grayer and less opaque, so what is underneath shows.
95: 28. A dark stroke laid into a wet pale passage lifts the pale and comes out
96:     paler than its pile.
97: 29. A passage laid against a wet neighbor drags the neighbor into its edge.
98: 30. Crossing strokes in wet paint thin each other at the crossings, and the
99:     layer below shows there.
100: 31. A tacky surface grabs: a brush dragged over it leaves its paint sooner
101:     and in broken patches (stick and slip).
102: 
103: ## Stippling
104: 
105: 32. Touches into a wet layer lift some of it and fuse. On a dry layer each
106:     touch stays separate.
107: 33. One dip serves one small patch of touches (24 by default), and each
108:     dip's mixture varies a little. On a dry layer the passage can dry as a
109:     patchwork of slightly different patches; fewer touches per dip make the
110:     patches smaller.
111: 34. Coverage is how many touches fall on each point; one touch covers about
112:     π(0.4 × width)².
113: 35. Contrast with what is underneath decides how a stipple reads. A coverage
114:     that gives a veil over a mid tone gives solid patches over a pale field.
115: 36. With `feather` above 0, touches press lighter where coverage falls
116:     below 1, so a thinning stipple ends in smaller, fainter marks; at 0 they
117:     keep their pressure.
118: 37. A row of separate touches along a thin line reads as a string of beads.
119:     A short dragged stroke along it reads as one continuous ridge.
120: 
121: ## Blending
122: 
123: 38. The blender fuses open paint by lifting it and moving it. It can't move
124:     set or dry paint.
125: 39. `blend` stays inside its mask by default. Unclipped, it drags wet paint
126:     across the mask's edge.
127:     A local blend can leave a seam where lifted or moved paint meets the
128:     untouched paint outside that mask. Inside a soft mask, wet dark and
129:     light passages still mix.
130: 40. Touches stippled into a wet layer and then blended fuse into it. Only
131:     the strongest contrasts survive, as thin traces. Touches laid after the
132:     blending pass stay on top as a lacy texture.
133: 41. Repeated blending of one lean layer lifts paint off the tops of the
134:     weave, and the ground shows through as a pale lattice.
135: 42. Blending spreads each thin spot in a layer into a soft-edged patch.
136: 
137: ## Glazing
138: 
139: 43. A brushed glaze (`hand="glaze"`) is unclipped.
140: 
141: ## Masks
142: 
143: 44. Every mask covers the whole canvas. A mask function that stays above
144:     zero far from the spot you mean paints there too.
145: 45. Masks from shapes (`poly`, `rect`, `ellipse`, `ribbon`) are crisp.
146:     `soften` and `blur` give them a ramp. `roughen` replaces the ramp with a
147:     new edge at the 0.5 level, so a long soft fade comes back as a hard
148:     edge.
149: 46. `ribbon` puts a round disc at every point, both ends included, so it
150:     reaches half a width past its end points.
151: 47. Two separately softened masks that meet leave a light gap or a dark
152:     overlap along the seam. A mask and its inverse (`m` and `-m`) meet
153:     without one.
154: 48. A passage bounded by a mask shows a cut edge wherever its paint differs
155:     from its neighbor's at the mask's edge.
156: 
157: ## Drying and time
158: 
159: 49. Paint goes from open (workable) to setting, tacky and touch-dry.
160:     Drying depends on pigment, thickness and oil; the guide describes
161:     the times at this easel.
162: 50. `wait` ages every point of the canvas at once. Which passages have set
163:     depends on their pigment, thickness and oil.
164: 51. A long pass is painted in 15-minute slices that age
165:     between them, so its first part is older than its last. While the work
166:     goes on, the paint under a later passage is still open and comes up
167:     into it.

170: 
171: 52. Graphite doesn't take on wet paint, and paint laid over it seals it.
172:     Thin paint lets a line show and body color hides it. Under a thin first
